readerTitle: Pitching a coffee brand: what makes investors lean in
caseNote: 가상 사례 (소규모 커피 로스터의 엔젤 투자 피치, 호텔 그룹 내부 팀의 예산 피치) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 커피 브랜드 피치는 맛과 열정이 아니라 재주문이라는 증거와 투자자가 돈을 돌려받는 경로로 설득한다. 회사 안의 예산 회의도 같은 질문을 던진다.
misconception: 좋은 제품 이야기와 큰 시장 규모를 보여주면 투자자는 설득된다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 ENT-04-03(투자자의 사고방식), ENT-04-05(트랙션)을 적용
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 가상입니다. 계산 확인: 카페 12곳 중 9곳 재주문 = 75%. 온라인 첫 구매자 500명 중 200명 재구매 = 40%. 업계 평균 재주문율 같은 실제 통계는 쓰지 않았습니다.
호텔 사례: 3개 호텔 8주 테스트, 전체 20개 호텔. 설문 70%는 가상의 응답률로, 실제 연구 수치가 아님을 확인하세요.
소비재 브랜드의 투자 회수 경로(대기업 인수, 배당)는 일반론으로만 적었습니다. 특정 기업 인수 사례나 수익률 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Ten minutes to pitch a coffee brand
body: Mina roasts coffee in a rented unit behind a bakery. She sells bags online and supplies 12 local cafés.
On Thursday she has ten minutes with three angel investors. She wants money for a bigger roaster. Everyone tells her to lead with the beans. The investors have tasted a lot of good coffee.

image.label: A small roaster with a laptop pitch deck beside coffee bags
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 로스팅 공간, 로스터 기계 옆 작업대 위에 노트북(피치 슬라이드)과 무지 원두 봉투들. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음. 따뜻한 조명.

cards.title: What should Mina open with?
body: She has one minute before attention drifts. Which opening gives the investors the most reason to keep listening?

options.text: Her story: how she fell for coffee and sources beans from small farms
options.feedback: A good story makes her memorable, but it proves nothing about demand. It works best right after the evidence, not instead of it.

options.text: The size of the coffee market and how many cups are drunk every day
options.feedback: Every coffee pitch can say this, so it tells investors nothing about her brand. A huge market says little about whether customers choose you.

options.text: Nine of her 12 cafés have reordered every month for six months
options.feedback: This is **traction**: proof that customers come back on their own. In coffee, the reorder is the signal that matters.

cards.title: Not all numbers count the same.
body: Mina listed everything she could show. Then she ranked it by how hard it would be to fake. Followers and first orders show curiosity. **Reorders at full price** show that customers want the coffee itself.

breakdown.label: First online orders
breakdown.detail: Many came from a launch discount

cards.softwareNote: A software founder faces the same test. Sign-ups are like first orders. Customers who keep paying month after month are the reorders investors look for.

cards.title: They're asking how their money comes back.
body: An angel isn't buying coffee. They're buying a share of a business and asking two things: how big can this get, and how do I get my money back?

For a coffee brand, the honest answer is rarely "the next global giant." It might be steady profits, or a sale to a larger food company one day. Investors respect a path they can believe more than a dream they can't.

cards.title: "Why is this worth my money?"
body: One investor leans back and asks it directly. How should Mina answer?

options.text: "If we win just 1% of the coffee market, we'll be huge."
options.feedback: It sounds modest, but it skips the hard part: how she wins any customers at all. Investors usually hear this as a sign the founder hasn't done the math.

options.text: "The new roaster triples capacity. At our current reorder rate, here's the path from 12 cafés to 40, and what that earns."
options.feedback: She links the money to what it unlocks and builds the plan from real numbers. That speaks to **how investors think**: a believable route to a return.

options.text: "Our coffee is better than anything else in town."
options.feedback: Quality matters, and her reorders back it up. But better coffee alone doesn't explain how the investor's money grows.

cards.title: Traction can be bought.
body: A heavy discount fills first orders fast. So does selling to friends who run cafés. Neither proves much.

Good investors will ask: did customers reorder at full price? Did strangers buy, not just people you know? If your best numbers came from a promotion, say so. Being caught hiding it costs more trust than the weak number ever would.

cards.title: Now you're pitching inside a company.
body: Daniel manages food and drink at a hotel group with 20 hotels. He wants budget to launch an in-house coffee brand for lobby cafés and rooms, with bags for guests to take home.
The finance committee meets next week. It decides which projects get money, so it thinks like an investor. What should he ask for?

image.label: A manager presenting to a small finance committee
image.brief: 회의실에서 한 매니저가 커피 봉투 샘플과 차트를 들고 세 명의 위원에게 발표하는 장면. 플랫 일러스트. 실제 호텔 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

options.text: Full budget for all 20 hotels, citing a survey where 70% of guests said they'd buy
options.feedback: The survey shows interest, but saying isn't buying. He'd be asking for the most money backed by the weakest kind of **traction**.

options.text: A small budget to test in 3 hotels for 8 weeks, tracking repeat café visits and take-home bag sales
options.feedback: He limits the downside and comes back with real buying behavior. The committee is comparing his project with other uses of the money, and this is **how investors think**.

options.text: A polished brand presentation with logo, packaging and a vision for the group
options.feedback: It looks impressive and answers none of the committee's questions. It spends effort on the story before there's any proof.

cards.title: Lead with proof, then show the path to a return.
body: Two ideas from this unit did the work. **Traction** (ENT-04-05): reorders at full price beat followers, first orders and surveys. **How investors think** (ENT-04-03): show how the money grows, and keep the downside small. They apply to an angel and to a budget committee alike.
**Try it today:** write down the one number that shows customers come back to you. If you don't have one, that's what to measure next.
